## Evidence map: radiologist views of peer review and peer learning

The literature includes national and specialty surveys, single-department attitude surveys, and evaluations of departments transitioning from score-based review to peer learning. The recurring distinction is between **support for learning and patient-care improvement** and concerns about **anonymity, blame, legal or career consequences, and workflow burden**.

| Study | Design and sample | Quantitative findings | What it suggests |
|---|---|---|---|
| **“Survey of radiologist attitudes and perceptions regarding the incorporation of a departmental peer review system” (2014; PMID 25439617)** | Questionnaire before implementation of a **nonanonymous** system at one academic hospital; 36 radiologists responded. | 86% considered peer review important for patient care and 81% for professional development. Yet 92% believed it should be anonymous; 72% worried it would not be safe from malpractice issues, 67% thought it could damage workplace relationships, and 42% thought it might affect job security or rankings. | Strong perceived educational and patient-care value coexisted with substantial anxiety about identifiable review. The study reported differences by years of experience. |
| **“Survey of faculty perceptions regarding a peer review system” (2014; PMID 24144835)** | Single-institution questionnaire; 50 of 52 faculty responded (96.2%); assessed an existing RADPEER-like system. | 44% agreed the system was a waste of time; 58% thought it was done merely to meet hospital or regulatory requirements. In contrast, 46% thought it improved radiologist performance, 32% thought it decreased medical error, and 42% saw value in protecting radiologists in medical-board cases. | Perceptions were mixed: perceived regulatory burden and limited value competed with professional, safety, and medico-legal benefits. |
| **“Survey of peer review programs among pediatric radiologists” (2019; PMID 30923884)** | Society of Pediatric Radiology member survey; 219 responses (15% of invitations), 80% from children’s hospitals. | 86% rated comment-enhanced feedback at least somewhat important to performance improvement, versus 48% for numerical scores. 68% rarely or never checked their numerical scores; 82% agreed comments were more effective feedback. 93% thought peer-learning conferences would benefit their practice; 48% thought their current system should be modified. | Respondents favored specific, explanatory feedback and educational conferences over score-centered systems; many saw room to improve existing programs. |
| **“Current State of Peer Learning in Radiology: A Survey of ACR Members” (2023; PMID 37230234)** | ACR member survey; 1,153 responses from 20,850 invitations (6%). | 610 respondents (53%) reported currently using peer learning and 334 (29%) reported not using it. Users were more often younger, female, and urban-practice radiologists than nonusers. | Peer learning had substantial but not universal uptake. The low response rate warrants caution when interpreting national prevalence or representativeness. |
| **“Transitioning to Peer Learning: Lessons Learned” (2021; PMID 33096087)** | Departmental before-and-after transition from traditional peer review to peer learning; staff surveyed after implementation. | Five significant discrepancies were submitted under the prior system versus 416 cases under peer learning. The most reported event types were perception (45.0%) and “great calls” (35.1%). The authors report that most surveyed radiologists felt peer learning offered more professional development and learning opportunities. | Changing the model was associated with much greater case participation and more positive reported educational value; this was a departmental implementation study, not a controlled comparison. |
| **“Peer learning is both preferable and less expensive than score-based peer review” (2024; PMID 38113549)** | Single tertiary academic center; Likert surveys before and after transition, with 27 radiologists in the reported preference analysis. | 70.4% (19/27) preferred peer learning and 25.9% (7/27) preferred the prior program. Positive-impact ratings were significantly higher and workflow-disruption ratings lower for peer learning. Reported time was 0.76 ± 0.45 hours/month for peer learning (n=27) versus 1.71 ± 1.84 hours/month for peer review (n=34; p=0.011). | In this center, preference favored peer learning, especially when respondents saw it as worth the investment; reported time burden was lower. |
| **“Converting case conferences to peer learning: Opportunities and barriers” (2025; PMID 39890515)** | Abdominal division pilot; faculty survey response rate 81%. | 88% favored a target of one submitted case per faculty member per month. All respondents considered a no-blame culture important; 70% favored anonymous case presentations. | Faculty support depended on psychological safety, but implementation faced practical barriers: workflow integration and time/ownership for a conference leader. |

### Related implementation evidence

Two transition studies help interpret the attitude findings, although their abstracts provide less detailed survey results. A department transitioning to peer collaborative improvement reviewed 12,197 cases and identified 1,140 learning opportunities; actively submitted cases had a much higher learning-opportunity yield than randomly reviewed cases (96.3% vs 3.88%) (**PMID 29055610**). An emergency-radiology peer-learning evaluation reported that all participants found the system easy to use and preferred it to peer review (**PMID 35391565**). These results are encouraging but are local program evaluations, not broad estimates of radiologist opinion.

### Synthesis and limitations

Across studies, radiologists commonly endorse peer review or peer learning as potentially useful for **patient care, professional development, and shared learning**. The strongest repeated preference is for **comments, discussion, and learning opportunities rather than isolated numerical scores**. The main concerns are **loss of anonymity, malpractice exposure, damage to collegial relationships, career consequences, regulatory box-checking, and the practical burden of integrating a program into workflow**. No-blame culture, clear educational purpose, and feasible processes appear important to acceptance.

The evidence is mostly self-reported and cross-sectional or from single-department implementation studies. Response rates vary substantially, and favorable post-transition perceptions do not by themselves establish improvement in patient outcomes. These studies should therefore be read as evidence about **reported attitudes and local experience**, not proof that one model is universally superior.

## Survey of radiologist attitudes toward departmental peer review

**Overall:** Radiologists generally recognize the potential value of peer review for patient care and professional development, but their support is conditional. Common reservations concern anonymity, blame, legal or career consequences, whether the process is genuinely educational, and the time it takes. Studies suggest many respondents prefer constructive feedback and peer learning over score-focused review.

| Survey or study | Main findings |
|---|---|
| **Departmental system survey** — 36 radiologists at one academic hospital (PMID: **25439617**) | 86% considered peer review important for patient care and 81% for professional development. At the same time, 92% believed review should be anonymous; 72% worried it would not be safe from malpractice issues, 67% anticipated harm to workplace relationships, and 42% worried about job security or rankings. |
| **Faculty perceptions of an existing system** — 50 respondents (PMID: **24144835**) | Views were mixed: 44% called the system a waste of time and 58% thought it was done mainly to satisfy hospital or regulatory requirements. Conversely, 46% thought it improved radiologist performance and 32% believed it reduced medical error. |
| **Pediatric radiologist survey** — 219 respondents (PMID: **30923884**) | 86% rated comment-enhanced feedback important for performance improvement, compared with 48% for numerical scores. 82% said comments were more effective feedback, and 93% thought peer-learning conferences could benefit their practice. |
| **ACR member survey** (PMID: **37230234**) | 53% of 1,153 respondents reported using peer learning. The response rate was only 6%, so the estimate may not represent all radiologists. |
| **Departmental transition to peer learning** — 27 radiologists in the preference analysis (PMID: **38113549**) | After a local transition, 70.4% preferred peer learning to the prior score-based program. This is encouraging but reflects one center, not a general preference estimate. |
| **Peer-learning pilot** (PMID: **39890515**) | All survey respondents considered a no-blame culture important, and 70% favored anonymous case presentations—evidence that implementation climate and safeguards matter. |

### Interpretation

The evidence points to **qualified support**, not unconditional enthusiasm. Radiologists appear more receptive when review is designed to help colleagues learn and improve care, rather than simply assign scores or fulfill a compliance requirement. Useful design principles suggested by the surveys include:

- Provide specific, explanatory feedback and opportunities for discussion.
- Establish a clear, nonpunitive learning purpose and a no-blame culture.
- Address confidentiality and perceived legal, employment, and collegial risks.
- Keep workflows feasible and communicate how cases and feedback will be used.

These findings are mainly self-reported, often from single institutions, and some surveys have limited response rates. They characterize reported attitudes; they do not establish that a particular peer-review model improves patient outcomes.

**Conclusion:** The survey literature suggests radiologists see value in departmental peer review, especially when it is constructive and educational, but acceptance depends on trust, psychological safety, and practical implementation.

FINAL DECISION: YES
